questions.stem: What is the relationship between third-party agent frameworks like LangGraph or Strands and Anthropic's own Claude Agent SDK?

options.text: They are mutually exclusive; using one means Claude cannot be used with the other

They represent alternative or complementary orchestration approaches for building agents with Claude, each with their own abstractions for control flow and state, layered on top of the same underlying model and API
LangGraph and Strands are Anthropic products that replace the Claude Agent SDK
They are only usable for non-Claude models

questions.explanation: Third-party frameworks and the native Agent SDK are alternative/complementary orchestration layers on top of the same underlying Claude API.

questions.stem: A team chooses to build a multi-agent system using LangGraph instead of the native Claude Agent SDK. What does this decision primarily reflect?

options.text: A requirement imposed by Anthropic for all production agents
An inability to use Claude's tool-use feature at all
A fundamentally different set of agent-design principles that don't apply to SDK-based agents
A build-tooling/orchestration choice layered on top of the same core agent-design principles (tool-use loops, subagents, memory) tested elsewhere in this domain

questions.explanation: The underlying agent-design principles remain the same; framework choice is an orchestration/tooling decision layered on top.

questions.stem: Which statement about agent design patterns (e.g., manager/subagent decomposition, memory management) across the native Agent SDK vs. third-party frameworks is most accurate?

options.text: These patterns are conceptually consistent across implementations, even though specific syntax and abstractions differ between the native SDK and frameworks like LangGraph or Strands
These patterns only apply to the native Claude Agent SDK and have no equivalent in third-party frameworks
Third-party frameworks cannot implement subagent architectures
Memory management is impossible outside the native SDK

questions.explanation: The core design patterns transfer conceptually across implementations; only the specific syntax/abstractions differ.

questions.stem: A team is already deeply invested in an existing LangGraph-based orchestration pipeline for multiple LLM providers and wants to add Claude as one of the models. What is a reasonable interpretation of this scenario?

options.text: LangGraph can integrate Claude as one of the models within its existing orchestration graph, without requiring a rewrite onto the native Agent SDK
They must abandon LangGraph and rebuild entirely on the Claude Agent SDK
Claude can only be used through its own SDK, never through third-party orchestration
This is not possible; LangGraph cannot be used with Claude

questions.explanation: Third-party frameworks can incorporate Claude as one of their supported models without forcing a rewrite onto Anthropic's native SDK.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable factor in choosing the native Claude Agent SDK over a third-party framework like Strands for a new, Claude-only agent project?

options.text: There is no valid reason to ever choose the native SDK
Tighter, more direct alignment with Claude-specific features without an additional abstraction layer, if the project doesn't need multi-provider or framework-specific orchestration features
Third-party frameworks cannot be used with Claude under any circumstances
The native SDK is the only option that supports tool use at all

questions.explanation: For Claude-only projects without a need for multi-provider orchestration, the native SDK avoids an extra abstraction layer.

questions.stem: Is it accurate that using a third-party agent framework means you can no longer apply concepts like stopping conditions, guardrails, or context management to your agent?

options.text: False, but only if the framework is LangGraph specifically
False — these are general agent-design concepts that still apply regardless of which orchestration layer (native SDK or third-party framework) implements the agent loop
True — these concepts are exclusive to the native Claude Agent SDK
True, but only for stopping conditions specifically

questions.explanation: Stopping conditions, guardrails, and context management are general agent-design concepts applicable regardless of the orchestration layer used.

questions.stem: Which requirement most favors a third-party agent framework over the native SDK?

options.text: The agent performs a single well-understood step
The project must remain portable across several model providers
The team wants the closest possible access to Claude-specific capabilities
The project targets Claude exclusively and needs minimal abstraction

questions.explanation: Multi-provider portability is a framework's central value. Claude-only projects wanting direct access to platform features are better served by the native SDK.

questions.stem: For an autonomous coding agent editing files, which design choice best balances autonomy with safety?

options.text: Give the agent unrestricted permissions so it never has to pause for approval
Define clear stopping conditions and human-approval checkpoints for high-impact actions, while allowing autonomy for low-risk steps
Disable all logging to improve performance
Never allow the agent to use any tools

questions.explanation: Well-designed agents combine autonomy for low-risk steps with explicit guardrails (approval checkpoints, stopping conditions) for higher-impact or irreversible actions.

questions.stem: An agent can issue refunds. Which guardrail design is soundest?

options.text: Instruct the agent in its system prompt never to exceed the refund limit
Use a more capable model tier so the limit is respected reliably
Enforce the limit in the refund service itself and require human approval above a threshold
Review a log of refunds weekly and reverse any that were incorrect

questions.explanation: Limits must be enforced where the action executes, since prompt instructions are not a security boundary. Human approval above a threshold bounds the damage of any single decision.

questions.stem: Why is a prompt instruction an inadequate guardrail for a high-impact action?

options.text: Instructions influence behavior but cannot guarantee it, so they do not constitute enforcement
Instructions are stripped from requests that define tools
Instructions only apply to the first turn of a conversation
Prompt instructions cannot describe constraints precisely enough

questions.explanation: Prompting shapes likely behavior; it does not make an action impossible. Anything that must not happen requires a technical control outside the model.

questions.stem: Select the TWO controls that meaningfully bound the risk of an autonomous agent with write access.

options.text: Increasing the iteration limit so the agent can self-correct
Scoping credentials so the agent can only reach the specific resources it needs
Adding a strongly worded warning to the system prompt
Requiring explicit human approval before irreversible operations

questions.explanation: Narrow credentials and approval gates on irreversible actions are enforceable controls. Prompt warnings are advisory, and more iterations expand rather than bound the blast radius.

questions.stem: In the Claude Agent SDK, what is the general purpose of the core query()-style interface?

options.text: It only formats text for display and has no role in agent execution
It replaces the need for any tool definitions
It drives the agent loop — sending messages, handling tool calls, and managing turns — so developers don't have to hand-roll that control flow themselves
It is used exclusively for evaluation, not for running agents

questions.explanation: The Agent SDK's core interface manages the agent loop (message exchange, tool call handling, turn management) so developers can build agents without reimplementing this control flow from scratch.

questions.stem: What does the Claude Agent SDK primarily provide over hand-rolling an agent against the raw API?

options.text: Ready-made handling of the agent loop, tool wiring, and session mechanics
Automatic elimination of token costs for tool calls
Exclusive access to models unavailable through the API
A guarantee that the agent cannot take unsafe actions

questions.explanation: The SDK packages the recurring scaffolding — loop control, tool integration, session handling — so teams are not rebuilding it. It confers no special model access or safety guarantee.

questions.stem: A team is writing its third bespoke agent loop and finding the retry, tool-dispatch, and history-management code repetitive. What does this suggest?

options.text: They should move the loop into the system prompt
They should switch to batch processing
Agents are the wrong architecture for the problem
The repeated scaffolding is what the Agent SDK exists to provide

questions.explanation: Repeatedly rebuilding loop plumbing is the signal to adopt the SDK, which supplies that layer and leaves the team to write only domain-specific tools and policy.

questions.stem: What role does context/memory management play in longer-running agent workflows?

options.text: Memory management only matters for single-turn, non-agentic requests
Agents automatically discard all context after each tool call, so no management is needed

As an agent takes many steps, developers often need strategies (e.g., summarizing prior steps, pruning irrelevant history) to keep the agent's context within limits and focused on relevant information
It is irrelevant since agents have unlimited context by default

questions.explanation: Long-running agents accumulate context over many steps; without active management (summarization, pruning) this can exceed context limits or dilute the model's focus with irrelevant history.

questions.stem: A long-running agent's context fills with verbose tool outputs, crowding out its objective. What is the most effective remedy?

options.text: Summarize or truncate tool results before appending them, retaining only decision-relevant fields
Remove the objective from context to make room for tool output
Disable tools once the context reaches a threshold
Restart the agent from scratch whenever context grows large

questions.explanation: Compacting tool output at the point of ingestion keeps the goal and salient state resident. Dropping the objective or restarting discards exactly what must persist.

questions.stem: Which state should an agent persist outside the conversation context?

options.text: Only the system prompt
Durable facts and progress that must survive compaction or a restart
Only the most recent tool result
Nothing; the context window is the correct place for all state

questions.explanation: Context is a working buffer that gets compacted and eventually lost. Anything that must survive belongs in external storage the agent can read back.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are legitimate reasons to build a custom agent loop instead of relying entirely on default SDK behavior?

options.text: You need fine-grained control over intermediate steps, such as custom logging, guardrails, or human-approval checkpoints between tool calls
You want to prevent the agent from ever using more than one tool call in total
Your application has domain-specific stopping conditions or retry logic not covered by default behavior
Custom agent loops are required before any tool can be defined

questions.explanation: Custom loops are useful when you need extra control (logging, guardrails, human-in-the-loop) or nonstandard stopping/retry logic — not for arbitrarily restricting tool-call counts or as a prerequisite for tool definitions.

questions.stem: What is the minimal cycle of a custom agent loop?

options.text: Call the model, execute any requested tools, append the results, and repeat until a termination condition holds
Send the request once and parse whatever comes back
Pre-plan every tool call, then execute them in a fixed order
Stream the response and terminate at the first content block

questions.explanation: The loop alternates model turns with tool execution, feeding results back until a stopping condition is met. Fixed pre-planned sequences are workflows, not agent loops.

questions.stem: An agent loop occasionally runs indefinitely, repeating the same tool call. Which safeguard addresses this most directly?

options.text: A maximum-iteration cap combined with detection of repeated no-progress states
A more capable model tier
Removing the tool from the agent's toolset
Increasing the output token ceiling

questions.explanation: Non-terminating loops need an explicit bound plus progress detection so repeated identical states break out. Model capability does not guarantee termination.

questions.stem: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. How should tool access be scoped for this agent?

options.text: Tools should be assigned randomly to test robustness
Limited to only the tools actually necessary for its task (least privilege), reducing risk if the agent misbehaves or is manipulated
Tool scoping doesn't matter since agents never misuse tools
Given access to every tool in the organization by default for flexibility

questions.explanation: Sound agent design for tool scoping in a multi-step travel-booking agent favors limited to only the tools actually necessary for its task (least privilege), reducing risk if the agent misbehaves or is manipulated

questions.stem: Which characteristic of a task most strongly indicates an agentic design rather than a fixed pipeline?

options.text: The task has high request volume
The task requires structured JSON output
The task must complete within a strict latency budget
The steps needed cannot be enumerated in advance and depend on what is discovered

questions.explanation: Agency is warranted when the path is data-dependent and cannot be scripted ahead of time. Volume, output shape, and latency constraints do not by themselves imply an agent.

questions.stem: You are designing a system with 2 specialized subagents coordinated by a manager/supervisor process. What is the primary benefit of this manager-subagent architecture?

options.text: It guarantees zero errors across the system
It allows decomposing a complex task into narrower, more focused subtasks, each handled by a subagent with tighter context and scope, improving reliability and manageability
It eliminates the need for any tool use
It removes the need for evaluation or testing

questions.explanation: Manager/subagent patterns decompose complex tasks so each subagent operates with a narrower, more focused context, generally improving reliability over one large monolithic agent.

questions.stem: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. How should this agent's overall goal best be broken down for reliability?

options.text: Into smaller, well-scoped subtasks (potentially via subagents) each with a narrower context, rather than one monolithic prompt trying to do everything at once
It should never be decomposed; one giant prompt is always more reliable
By decomposing it into subtasks written in a different programming language
Decomposition is irrelevant to agent reliability

questions.explanation: Sound agent design for decomposition in a multi-step travel-booking agent favors into smaller, well-scoped subtasks (potentially via subagents) each with a narrower context, rather than one monolithic prompt trying to do everything at once

questions.stem: What is the primary benefit of delegating subtasks to subagents rather than handling everything in one context?

options.text: Subagents remove the need for tool definitions
Each subagent works in its own context with a narrow remit, keeping the manager's context focused
Subagents eliminate token costs for delegated work
Subagents guarantee deterministic results

questions.explanation: Delegation partitions context and responsibility, so detail stays with the specialist and the manager retains an uncluttered view of overall progress.

questions.stem: A manager agent coordinates six subagents and results are becoming inconsistent and hard to trace. Which corrective step is most useful?

options.text: Sharpen each subagent's remit and define the contract for what it returns to the manager
Merge all subagents back into a single agent
Give every subagent access to the full toolset for flexibility
Increase the manager's iteration limit

questions.explanation: Inconsistency across delegates usually traces to fuzzy responsibilities and undefined return contracts. Tightening both restores traceability without abandoning decomposition.

questions.stem: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. What should determine when this agent decides it has completed its task and should stop?

options.text: Running forever until manually killed
An arbitrary fixed number of turns with no relation to task completion
Explicit, well-defined completion/stopping criteria tied to the task's actual goal (not just an arbitrary step limit) so the agent halts at the right point
Never stopping, since agents should always keep iterating

questions.explanation: Sound agent design for stopping conditions in a multi-step travel-booking agent favors explicit, well-defined completion/stopping criteria tied to the task's actual goal (not just an arbitrary step limit) so the agent halts at the right point

questions.stem: What should determine when an agent stops working on a task?

options.text: When the model stops requesting tools, with no additional bound
A fixed number of iterations chosen for every task alike
When the context window is exhausted
Whichever comes first: satisfaction of an explicit success condition, or a safety bound such as an iteration or budget cap

questions.explanation: Sound termination pairs a definition of done with a backstop bound, so the agent halts on success or on exhausting its allowance rather than drifting.

questions.stem: Why is 'the model produced no further tool calls' insufficient as the sole stopping condition?

options.text: Tool calls are always present in every response
The absence of a tool call cannot be detected programmatically
The model may stop calling tools without having achieved the objective
Stopping requires an explicit stop sequence to be configured

questions.explanation: Ceasing to call tools indicates the model has nothing further to try, not that the goal was met. Verification against a success condition is what distinguishes completion from giving up.

questions.stem: What is the key distinction between a 'workflow' and an 'agent' in the context of building with Claude?

options.text: There is no meaningful distinction; the terms are interchangeable
A workflow follows a predefined sequence of steps orchestrated by the developer, while an agent dynamically decides its own steps/tool calls based on the model's reasoning
Agents never use tools, while workflows always use tools
Workflows can only be built with the Claude Agent SDK, and agents cannot

questions.explanation: Workflows are developer-orchestrated fixed sequences; agents use the model to dynamically plan and execute steps, including deciding which tools to call and when to stop.

questions.stem: You are designing a warehouse-robotics coordination agent and must decide between a fixed, developer-orchestrated workflow versus a fully autonomous agent that plans its own steps. Which factor most strongly favors the fixed-workflow approach?

options.text: The task is extremely open-ended with highly variable steps that can't be predicted in advance
There is no meaningful difference; the choice should be arbitrary
The team wants maximum flexibility for handling unexpected edge cases
The task's steps are well-understood, predictable, and rarely vary — reducing the value of dynamic planning while increasing the value of predictable, auditable execution

questions.explanation: Fixed, predictable, well-understood tasks generally favor a developer-orchestrated workflow (more predictable and auditable); highly variable, open-ended tasks favor a dynamically planning agent.

questions.stem: A document pipeline always performs extract, then validate, then file — never varying. Which design is appropriate?

options.text: A manager agent with three subagents
An autonomous agent that decides the order at runtime
A developer-orchestrated workflow with the three steps in fixed sequence
A single request with all three instructions concatenated

questions.explanation: A known, invariant sequence is best expressed as an explicit workflow: more predictable, cheaper, and easier to debug than granting runtime discretion that is never needed.

questions.stem: Select the TWO costs of choosing an autonomous agent where a fixed workflow would suffice.

options.text: Less predictable execution paths, making behavior harder to test and reason about
Loss of the ability to define custom tools
Inability to return structured output
Additional model calls for planning and reflection that the fixed path would not incur

questions.explanation: Unnecessary agency buys variability and extra deliberation cost. Neither tool definitions nor structured output is affected by the choice.

questions.stem: Your application needs to process 10 independent, non-urgent requests (e.g., overnight classification) where turnaround of a few hours is acceptable. What is the most appropriate integration approach?

options.text: Send all requests synchronously in a tight loop as fast as possible
Use the Message Batches API to submit the requests as a batch job at a lower cost
Open one long-lived streaming connection for all requests simultaneously
Manually shard the requests across multiple API keys to bypass rate limits

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is designed for large volumes of non-latency-sensitive requests and offers reduced cost compared to synchronous calls.

questions.stem: You are translating a product requirement — 'a real-time chat feature' — into a technical integration plan. Which factor should most directly influence your choice between synchronous (real-time) calls and the Batches API?

options.text: The programming language used by the frontend
Whether the use case requires an immediate response (latency-sensitive) or can tolerate delayed, asynchronous processing
The number of engineers on the team
Whether the application uses TypeScript or Python

questions.explanation: Latency sensitivity is the key driver: real-time, user-facing interactions need synchronous calls; bulk/delay-tolerant work suits the Batches API.

questions.stem: Roughly what cost reduction does the Message Batches API offer relative to equivalent synchronous requests?

options.text: No reduction; batching only changes latency
About 10%
About 50%
About 90%

questions.explanation: Batch processing is priced at roughly half the cost of the equivalent synchronous calls, which is the main reason to choose it for delay-tolerant volume.

questions.stem: You submit a batch and need to match each result back to the row of your database that produced it. What mechanism supports this?

options.text: You must submit one request per batch to keep the mapping unambiguous
Results are returned in exactly the submission order, so you can zip them positionally
You re-send the original prompt text and match on string equality
Each request carries a caller-supplied custom identifier that is echoed on its result

questions.explanation: Each request in a batch carries a caller-assigned identifier that comes back attached to the corresponding result, so results can be reassociated without relying on ordering.

questions.stem: A batch has been submitted but not all requests have finished. What is true of the results?

options.text: Nothing is retrievable until every request in the batch reaches a terminal state
The batch is automatically cancelled if any single request fails
Partial results are streamed back continuously as each request completes
Failed requests silently disappear from the result set

questions.explanation: A batch is retrieved once processing has ended; individual requests reach terminal states and the results become available as a set rather than as a live stream.

questions.stem: Select the TWO scenarios that are appropriate for the Message Batches API.

options.text: Generating the reply in a live chat widget while the user waits
Re-classifying a 400,000-row archive of historical support tickets overnight
Producing embeddings-style bulk annotations for a data warehouse refresh that runs nightly
Streaming a token-by-token response into a code editor's autocomplete

questions.explanation: Batch suits high-volume, delay-tolerant work (B and C). A and D are latency-critical and interactive, where a synchronous or streaming request is required.

questions.stem: What does enabling citations on a document content block allow an application to do?

options.text: Compress the document to reduce token usage
Automatically translate the document into another language
Convert the document into an image for vision processing
Ground specific claims in Claude's response back to precise locations in the source document, enabling traceable, source-linked answers

questions.explanation: Citations ground specific claims back to precise source locations, enabling traceable, source-linked answers.

questions.stem: How does the citations feature differ from simply instructing Claude in the prompt to 'cite your sources'?

options.text: Prompt-based citation instructions are always more reliable than the citations feature
There is no difference; both produce identical guarantees

Citations is a structured, API-level feature tied to the document content block that grounds claims to specific source locations, rather than relying on the model to informally mention a source in free text
Citations can only be used with images, never documents

questions.explanation: Citations is a structured, API-level grounding mechanism, distinct from and more reliable than an informal prompt instruction to 'cite sources.'

questions.stem: A compliance tool needs every factual claim in Claude's output to be traceable to an exact location in the source regulatory document. Which feature is most directly suited to this requirement?

options.text: The Batches API
Extended thinking
The citations feature on the document content block
Prompt caching

questions.explanation: Citations is purpose-built for grounding claims to exact source locations, matching this compliance requirement directly.

questions.stem: Which application would benefit LEAST from enabling citations?

options.text: A compliance-review tool grounding findings in regulatory text
A legal research tool needing to show exactly where in a case file a claim came from
A research assistant summarizing a scientific paper with source-linked claims
A casual creative-writing brainstorming assistant with no source documents involved

questions.explanation: Citations only add value when there's a source document to ground claims in; a source-free creative brainstorming task has nothing to cite.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable design choice for an application when citations are enabled and Claude's response includes several grounded claims?

options.text: Citations cannot be surfaced to end users under any circumstances
Prevent the user from ever seeing which document a claim came from
Surface the citation information to the end user (e.g., as inline references or links back to the source location) so they can verify claims
Discard the citation information entirely and show plain text only

questions.explanation: Surfacing citation data to end users (inline references, source links) is the natural way to realize citations' verifiability benefit.

questions.stem: Do citations require the underlying content to be provided as a special image format rather than as a standard document content block?

options.text: False, but only because citations don't exist
True, but only for PDFs specifically
True — citations only work on images
False — citations are tied to document (and similar text-bearing) content blocks, not a special image-only format

questions.explanation: Citations work with document/text-bearing content blocks, not a special image-only format.

questions.stem: A compliance team needs every assertion in a generated summary to be traceable to an exact location in the source filing. Which approach best meets this?

options.text: Append 'always cite your sources' to the system prompt and parse the model's freeform references
Enable the citations feature on the document content block and render the returned source locations
Ask for a bibliography at the end of the response
Lower temperature so the model quotes the document more literally

questions.explanation: Citations is an API-level feature on the document block that returns structured references to precise source locations, which is verifiable in a way that prompt-level instructions are not.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the citations feature from simply instructing the model to cite its sources?

options.text: Citations works without providing any source document
Citations returns structured references tied to the supplied document rather than model-generated prose references
Citations is only available in batch mode
Citations replaces the need to validate output entirely

questions.explanation: The feature yields structured, machine-readable references anchored to the document you supplied, which is why they can be displayed and checked; prompt-level requests produce prose that may itself be fabricated.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for maintaining conversation history (prior turns) across multiple calls to the Messages API?

options.text: History can only be maintained using the Batches API
History is never needed since Claude has persistent memory across all API calls by default
The calling application, which must include the full relevant message history in each request
Anthropic's servers automatically persist and inject full history for you

questions.explanation: The Claude API is stateless between calls; the application must resend the conversation history it wants considered on each request.

questions.stem: The Messages API is stateless. What follows for a multi-turn chat application?

options.text: The application must resend the relevant prior turns with each new request
The API retains the last ten turns per API key automatically
State is preserved as long as the same model is used
Conversation history is stored server-side and referenced by conversation id

questions.explanation: Because the endpoint holds no session state, the caller owns the history and must include the prior turns it wants the model to condition on.

questions.stem: A long-running assistant thread is approaching the model's context limit. Which strategy preserves continuity most economically?

options.text: Drop the system prompt to free room for more conversation
Truncate the most recent turns, since older context is more authoritative
Start a fresh conversation with no carryover on every request
Summarize older turns into a compact recap and keep recent turns verbatim

questions.explanation: Compacting distant history into a summary while retaining recent turns verbatim keeps the salient state within budget. Dropping the system prompt or the newest turns discards the most load-bearing context.

questions.stem: In a tool-using conversation, what must the application include when continuing after the model requests a tool call?

options.text: A fresh conversation seeded with just the tool output
The tool result with a newly generated identifier of the caller's choosing
Only the tool's output, with the assistant turn omitted
The assistant turn containing the tool request, followed by a user turn carrying the matching tool result

questions.explanation: The assistant's tool-request turn stays in the history and is answered by a result block whose identifier matches the request, so the model can tie the output to the call it made.

questions.stem: What is the effect of prefilling the beginning of the assistant's turn in the messages array?

options.text: It is rejected as malformed, since only user turns may be supplied
It steers the continuation to follow the supplied opening, which is useful for enforcing a format
It causes the model to repeat the prefill verbatim and then stop
It resets any system prompt already in effect

questions.explanation: Supplying the start of the assistant turn constrains what follows, a common technique for forcing a response to open in a required shape.

questions.stem: Two users of a chat product occasionally see fragments of each other's conversations. Which application-side defect best explains this?

options.text: Conversation history is being kept in a process-wide structure rather than scoped per session
The model's context window is too small for concurrent use
The API is leaking state between requests sharing an API key
Streaming was enabled for both sessions simultaneously

questions.explanation: Since the API holds no state, cross-talk originates in the application's own history storage — typically history held in shared or global scope instead of per-session.

questions.stem: An application receives repeated HTTP 400 responses from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.text: Recognize that 400 indicates a malformed or invalid request, and handle it accordingly (e.g., exponential backoff for rate/overload errors, fixing the request for client errors)
Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
Ignore the error code and simply resend the identical request in a tight loop
Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code

questions.explanation: HTTP 400 specifically indicates a malformed or invalid request; production applications should branch handling logic on status code rather than treating all errors alike.

questions.stem: An application receives repeated HTTP 401 responses from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.text: Ignore the error code and simply resend the identical request in a tight loop
Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code

Recognize that 401 indicates an authentication failure (invalid or missing API key), and handle it accordingly (e.g., exponential backoff for rate/overload errors, fixing the request for client errors)
Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers

questions.explanation: HTTP 401 specifically indicates an authentication failure (invalid or missing API key); production applications should branch handling logic on status code rather than treating all errors alike.

questions.stem: An application receives repeated HTTP 429 responses from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.text: Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code
Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers

Recognize that 429 indicates the caller has exceeded a rate limit and should back off and retry, and handle it accordingly (e.g., exponential backoff for rate/overload errors, fixing the request for client errors)
Ignore the error code and simply resend the identical request in a tight loop

questions.explanation: HTTP 429 specifically indicates the caller has exceeded a rate limit and should back off and retry; production applications should branch handling logic on status code rather than treating all errors alike.

questions.stem: An application receives repeated HTTP 500 responses from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.text: Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
Recognize that 500 indicates an unexpected server-side error, and handle it accordingly (e.g., exponential backoff for rate/overload errors, fixing the request for client errors)
Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code
Ignore the error code and simply resend the identical request in a tight loop

questions.explanation: HTTP 500 specifically indicates an unexpected server-side error; production applications should branch handling logic on status code rather than treating all errors alike.

questions.stem: An application receives repeated HTTP 529 responses from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.text: Recognize that 529 indicates the API is temporarily overloaded, and handle it accordingly (e.g., exponential backoff for rate/overload errors, fixing the request for client errors)
Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
Ignore the error code and simply resend the identical request in a tight loop
Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code

questions.explanation: HTTP 529 specifically indicates the API is temporarily overloaded; production applications should branch handling logic on status code rather than treating all errors alike.

questions.stem: A team wants to integrate Claude into a Python codebase. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Claude can only be accessed through a graphical interface, never programmatically
Raw HTTP calls to the API are blocked and require an SDK
Only Python is capable of calling the Claude API
Official client SDKs exist for common languages, and for any language the underlying Messages API can be called directly over HTTP

questions.explanation: Anthropic provides official SDKs for common languages, and since the API is a standard HTTP/JSON interface, any language capable of making HTTP requests can integrate directly.

questions.stem: A client is being rate limited. Which retry behavior is most appropriate?

options.text: Switch to a different model on every retry attempt
Fail the user's request permanently on the first rate-limit response
Back off with increasing delays and jitter, honoring any retry-after guidance in the response
Retry immediately in a tight loop until a request succeeds

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter, respecting retry-after guidance, drains the queue without amplifying congestion. Tight retry loops make the limit worse.

questions.stem: Select the TWO status codes for which retrying the identical request is a reasonable strategy.
questions.explanation: Rate limiting and temporary overload are transient, so the same request may succeed later. A malformed request and an authentication failure require fixing the request or the credentials; retrying unchanged cannot help.

questions.stem: When extended thinking is enabled for a request, which statement is accurate?

options.text: Extended thinking replaces the need for a system prompt
Thinking content is never returned to the client under any circumstances
The model can produce an internal reasoning process before its final answer, and this consumes part of the token budget
Extended thinking eliminates all token costs for the response

questions.explanation: Extended thinking allows the model to reason before answering, and thinking tokens count toward usage/cost considerations.

questions.stem: How is the depth of extended thinking controlled on a request?

options.text: It cannot be controlled; the model decides unilaterally
By setting a token budget for the thinking portion of the response
By selecting a dedicated reasoning-only endpoint
By raising temperature until reasoning appears

questions.explanation: Extended thinking is configured with a token budget for the reasoning portion, making depth an explicit request-level cost/quality decision.

questions.stem: A team enables extended thinking on every request in a high-volume classification pipeline and costs rise sharply with no accuracy gain. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: Extended thinking is incompatible with classification and returns invalid output
The thinking budget should be raised further to see a benefit
The cost increase is unrelated to thinking and must come from caching
Thinking tokens are billed, and simple pattern-matching tasks rarely benefit from deliberation

questions.explanation: Reasoning tokens are billed like other output, so enabling deliberation on tasks that do not require it adds cost without quality benefit. It is a targeted tool, not a global default.

questions.stem: Which task profile is the strongest candidate for extended thinking?

options.text: Extracting a phone number from a fixed-format record
Reconciling a multi-step financial calculation with interacting constraints
Translating a single sentence into French
Echoing a supplied string in uppercase

questions.explanation: Deliberation pays off where the answer depends on several interacting steps that benefit from working through. Mechanical single-step transformations gain nothing.

questions.stem: When continuing a tool-use conversation in which extended thinking was enabled, how should the prior thinking content be handled?

options.text: Rewrite the thinking blocks into a shorter paraphrase
Strip all thinking blocks before sending the next request
Preserve the returned thinking blocks in the conversation history as they were received
Move the thinking content into the system prompt

questions.explanation: Thinking blocks are returned as part of the assistant turn and are passed back unmodified when continuing the exchange, so the model retains the reasoning that led to its tool request.

questions.stem: Where does extended thinking output appear in a response?

options.text: In an HTTP header
Interleaved silently into the text block with no marker
Only in the usage object as a token count
As a distinct content block preceding the final text

questions.explanation: Reasoning is returned as its own content block ahead of the answer, which is what lets an application choose whether to display, log, or hide it.

questions.stem: Which statement about sending plain text to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.text: plain text cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances
plain text can be included as typed content blocks within a message, alongside text
plain text require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
plain text can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API

questions.explanation: The Messages API supports multiple typed content blocks (text, image, document, etc.) within a single message.

questions.stem: A team wants to integrate Claude from a language with no official SDK. What is the most direct path?

options.text: Call the HTTP/JSON endpoints directly from that language
Rewrite the service in a language that has an official SDK
Route calls through a browser automation harness
Wait for an official SDK, since direct HTTP access is not supported

questions.explanation: The API is a standard HTTP/JSON interface, so any language capable of issuing HTTP requests can integrate without an SDK.

questions.stem: Where should an API key live in a production deployment?

options.text: In the client-side bundle so the browser can call the API directly and reduce hops
Committed to the repository so every environment stays in sync
In server-side configuration or a secret manager, with requests proxied through your backend
Embedded in the mobile binary, obfuscated

questions.explanation: Keys must stay server-side in configuration or a secret store, with the application proxying calls; anything shipped to a client is retrievable by users.

questions.stem: Which statement about sending base64-encoded images to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.text: base64-encoded images cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances
base64-encoded images require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
base64-encoded images can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API
base64-encoded images can be included as typed content blocks within a message, alongside text

questions.explanation: The Messages API supports multiple typed content blocks (text, image, document, etc.) within a single message.

questions.stem: Which statement about sending PDF documents to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.text: PDF documents can be included as typed content blocks within a message, alongside text
PDF documents require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
PDF documents can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API
PDF documents cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances

questions.explanation: The Messages API supports multiple typed content blocks (text, image, document, etc.) within a single message.

questions.stem: Which statement about sending multiple images in one message to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.text: multiple images in one message require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
multiple images in one message can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API
multiple images in one message can be included as typed content blocks within a message, alongside text
multiple images in one message cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances

questions.explanation: The Messages API supports multiple typed content blocks (text, image, document, etc.) within a single message.

questions.stem: A developer wants Claude to analyze a screenshot of a UI bug. What is the correct way to include this in a Messages API request?

options.text: As an image content block (e.g. base64-encoded) within the same message alongside any accompanying text
As a separate, unrelated API call using a different endpoint entirely
By embedding a URL directly in the system prompt text with no special formatting
Images cannot be analyzed by Claude under any API configuration

questions.explanation: Vision input is provided as typed image content blocks within a message, which can be combined with text blocks in the same request.

questions.stem: An invoice-processing service receives scanned PDFs and must extract line items. What is the most direct integration?

options.text: Send the PDF as a document content block in the same Messages request as the extraction instruction
Run a separate OCR service first, since the API accepts text only
Convert the PDF to a spreadsheet before sending it
Call a dedicated document endpoint distinct from Messages

questions.explanation: PDFs are supplied as document content blocks alongside the text instruction in an ordinary Messages request; there is no separate document endpoint.

questions.stem: Select the TWO accurate statements about multimodal requests.

options.text: Multiple images can be included in a single message alongside text
Images must be sent to a separate vision endpoint before the text request
Only one content block of any type is permitted per message
Image content blocks may be supplied as base64-encoded data

questions.explanation: Messages accept several content blocks of mixed types, and images can be provided as base64 data. There is no separate vision endpoint, and messages are not limited to a single block.

questions.stem: Image-heavy requests in a document pipeline are consuming far more tokens than expected. Which factor most directly explains this?

options.text: Image dimensions drive token consumption, so large images cost substantially more than downscaled ones
Base64 encoding is billed at double the rate of binary upload
Only the file name is tokenized, so cost should be negligible
Images are billed per request rather than per token, so volume is irrelevant

questions.explanation: An image's token cost scales with its dimensions, so downscaling to the smallest size that preserves the detail you need is the main lever on cost.

questions.stem: You are building a customer support widget that must handle a static 5,000-token system prompt on every request while user input varies. What should you do to reduce latency and cost?

options.text: Send the system prompt as a separate API call before each user turn
Enable prompt caching on the static system prompt content
Truncate the system prompt to 500 tokens
Switch to synchronous polling instead of a single request

questions.explanation: Prompt caching lets repeated static content (like a large system prompt) be reused across calls without being reprocessed and re-billed at full price each time.

questions.stem: How do the costs of a cache write and a cache read compare to an ordinary uncached input token?

options.text: A write costs somewhat more than an uncached token; a read costs a small fraction of one
A write is free and a read is billed at the full rate
Both cost the same as an uncached token; only latency improves
Both are cheaper than an uncached token

questions.explanation: Establishing the cache carries a premium over normal input pricing, while subsequent reads of that prefix are billed at a small fraction, which is why caching only pays off when the prefix is reused.

questions.stem: Caching was enabled on a large system prompt, but the hit rate is near zero. The prompt ends with the current timestamp. What is the problem?

options.text: The timestamp changes the cached prefix on every call, so no request matches a stored one
Caching cannot be applied to system prompts
Timestamps are stripped automatically, so the cause must lie elsewhere
The cache requires the whole request, not just a prefix, to be identical

questions.explanation: A cache hit needs an exact prefix match. Volatile content inside the cached span invalidates it every call; such content belongs after the cache breakpoint.

questions.stem: Where should a cache breakpoint be placed in a request containing tool definitions, a long static system prompt, and a short variable user question?

options.text: Between the tool definitions and the system prompt only
After the tool definitions and system prompt, before the user question
After the user question, at the end of the request
At the very start of the request, before the tool definitions

questions.explanation: The breakpoint goes at the end of the stable span so tools and the static system prompt are cached while the varying question stays outside the cached prefix.

questions.stem: How can an application confirm that prompt caching is actually taking effect?

options.text: By enabling streaming, which emits a cache-hit event
Caching is opaque and cannot be observed from the response
By comparing wall-clock latency across runs, the only available signal
By reading cache creation and cache read token counts reported in the response usage data

questions.explanation: Usage data reports tokens written to and read from the cache, which is the direct measurement of whether the breakpoint is working.

questions.stem: A cached prefix stops being reused after a quiet period in a low-traffic application. What explains this?

options.text: Low traffic increases the minimum cacheable length
Cache entries expire after a period of inactivity
Caches persist indefinitely, so the cause must be a prompt change
Caches are invalidated whenever the API key is used from a new IP

questions.explanation: Cache entries have a limited lifetime that refreshes on use, so sparse traffic can let an entry lapse between requests.

questions.stem: Select the TWO conditions under which prompt caching delivers meaningful savings.

options.text: Each request contains entirely new text with no shared prefix
A large reference document is resent unchanged across many requests
A lengthy static system prompt precedes a short varying user message on every call
Requests are large but each is issued exactly once

questions.explanation: Savings require a substantial prefix that repeats across calls. Content that is unique per request, or large but never reused, cannot produce cache reads.

questions.stem: An API response comes back with stop_reason = 'end_turn'. What does this tell the calling application?

options.text: The request failed and should be retried
stop_reason is only informational and never affects application logic
The reason generation halted, which determines what the application should do next (e.g., resume, execute a tool, or treat the turn as complete)
The model has permanently ended the conversation and no further requests are possible

questions.explanation: stop_reason tells the application why generation stopped (e.g. 'tool_use' means the app should execute a tool and return results; 'max_tokens' may mean the app should continue the generation).

questions.stem: A response is unexpectedly cut off mid-sentence with stop_reason 'max_tokens'. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Lower the temperature parameter
Increase the max_tokens value for the request (and/or continue generation in a follow-up call)
Switch to the Batches API
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt

questions.explanation: 'max_tokens' as a stop reason means the output hit its length ceiling; raising the max_tokens parameter or continuing the generation resolves the truncation.

questions.stem: A response returns with a stop reason indicating the token ceiling was reached. What should the application do?

options.text: Recognize the output is incomplete and either raise the ceiling or request a continuation
Treat the partial output as final and display it
Retry the identical request, since the result is nondeterministic
Discard the output and report a server error to the user

questions.explanation: Hitting the ceiling means the output was cut off mid-generation. The fix is a larger budget or an explicit continuation, not treating truncated text as a finished answer.

questions.stem: A response's stop reason indicates the model wants to use a tool. What does this signal about the conversation?

options.text: The tool has already run and its output is in the text block
It has paused awaiting the application to execute the tool and return a result
The request failed validation and must be resubmitted
It has ended and no further turns are possible

questions.explanation: That stop reason is a handoff: the model has produced a tool request and is waiting for the application to execute it and supply the result so the exchange can continue.

questions.stem: An application configured a stop sequence and now sees responses ending earlier than intended. What is the likely cause?

options.text: Stop sequences are advisory and cannot end generation
The model ignores stop sequences when tools are defined
The configured string occurs naturally in the generated content, halting output there
Stop sequences apply only to the system prompt

questions.explanation: Generation halts at the first occurrence of a configured stop string, so a sequence that appears naturally in normal output will truncate responses unintentionally.

questions.stem: Why is branching on the stop reason preferable to inspecting only the text content of a response?

options.text: Different terminations demand different follow-up actions that the text alone does not distinguish
Text content is unavailable unless streaming is enabled
The stop reason is the only field that contains the model's answer
The stop reason guarantees the response is factually correct

questions.explanation: Natural completion, truncation, a stop-sequence halt, and a tool request all require different handling, and the text alone does not reliably distinguish them.

questions.stem: When consuming a streamed response, which correctly describes the relationship between the 'message_start' and 'content_block_start' events?

options.text: 'message_start' always arrives after 'content_block_start' regardless of stream order
Both are part of the ordered sequence of server-sent events that together let the client reconstruct the full message incrementally
Only one of these two events is ever emitted in a given stream
These events are unrelated to streaming and only appear in non-streaming responses

questions.explanation: Claude's streaming API emits an ordered sequence of SSE events (message_start, content_block_start/delta/stop, message_delta, message_stop) that the client accumulates to reconstruct the full response.

questions.stem: A client renders streamed output but the final text is missing fragments. Which implementation error is most likely?

options.text: Requesting streaming without also raising the token ceiling
Rendering each delta event in isolation instead of accumulating them in order
Failing to poll the endpoint frequently enough between events
Using a single HTTP connection rather than one per event

questions.explanation: Streamed responses arrive as ordered incremental deltas that the client accumulates into the full message; treating each event as a standalone value loses content.

questions.stem: Which best characterizes how streaming is requested and delivered?

options.text: The client polls a job identifier until the response is ready
A separate streaming endpoint returns a WebSocket handle
The response arrives as a single JSON object with an array of deltas
A parameter on the ordinary Messages request switches the response to a sequence of server-sent events

questions.explanation: Streaming is a flag on the normal Messages request; the response then arrives as a server-sent event stream rather than one blocking payload.

questions.stem: During a long stream, a client sees periodic events carrying no content. How should these be handled?

options.text: Treated as keep-alive traffic and ignored for rendering purposes
Treated as end-of-message markers
Treated as errors requiring the stream to be restarted
Rendered as blank lines to preserve fidelity

questions.explanation: Contentless events keep the connection alive during generation gaps; a robust client ignores unrecognized or empty event types rather than failing on them.

questions.stem: An error occurs after a stream has already begun emitting text. How does this surface?

options.text: As an error event within the stream, after content has already been delivered
As a silent connection close with no indication
As a non-200 HTTP status on the original request
It cannot happen; errors only occur before the first event

questions.explanation: The HTTP response has already succeeded by then, so mid-stream failures arrive as an error event inside the stream, which clients must handle alongside content events.

questions.stem: Which requirement most strongly favors streaming over a single blocking response?

options.text: A pipeline that needs the complete response before any downstream step
A request that must be retried automatically on failure
A conversational UI where users should see output begin within a moment
A nightly job writing results to a database with no user waiting

questions.explanation: Streaming reduces perceived latency where a human is watching output appear. Batch and pipeline work that needs the whole response first gains nothing from it.

questions.stem: You're integrating Claude into a retail chatbot and need the response to include both a natural-language explanation and a machine-readable structured result in one turn. What is the most robust approach?

options.text: Make two completely separate, uncoordinated API calls and hope the outputs match
Structured output is impossible with the Claude API
Instruct the model (with a clear format spec and example) to return both parts in a single well-defined structure, such as explanatory text followed by a clearly delimited JSON block
Only use the Batches API, since synchronous calls cannot return structured data

questions.explanation: A single request with a clear, well-specified output format (and an example) is the standard way to reliably get both natural-language and structured content from one call.

questions.stem: A service needs JSON conforming to a fixed schema and occasionally receives prose wrapped around the object. Which combination is the most robust fix?

options.text: Constrain the shape via a schema-bearing tool definition, then validate and retry on failure
Lower temperature to zero, which guarantees schema conformance
Switch to a larger model and accept the output unvalidated
Raise the token ceiling and retry until prose stops appearing

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained tool input plus application-side validation with retry is the durable pattern. Sampling changes reduce but never eliminate malformed output, so validation remains necessary.

questions.stem: Why is tool use a practical mechanism for obtaining structured data even when no external action is performed?

options.text: Tool calls bypass the model's token budget
Tool results are validated server-side before being returned
Tool inputs are schema-defined, so the model's output is shaped by that schema
Tool definitions are cached automatically and cost nothing

questions.explanation: A tool definition carries an input schema, so requesting a tool call is a way of asking for schema-shaped output — a widely used pattern even when the 'tool' only captures data.

questions.stem: An extraction service must handle documents where a required field is genuinely absent. What schema design best prevents fabricated values?

options.text: Make every field required so the model always returns something
Allow an explicit null or not-found value for the field and instruct the model to use it
Omit the field from the schema entirely
Retry with a higher temperature until a plausible value appears

questions.explanation: Giving the model a legitimate way to report absence removes the pressure to invent a value. Forcing every field to be populated actively encourages fabrication.

questions.stem: An application defines a tool named 'get_weather' in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.text: Claude may respond with a request to call 'get_weather' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message
Claude executes 'get_weather' directly against the live backend itself
Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
'get_weather' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement

questions.explanation: Claude does not execute tools itself — it emits a tool_use request, and the calling application executes the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result content block.

questions.stem: An application defines a tool named 'lookup_inventory' in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.text: Claude may respond with a request to call 'lookup_inventory' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message
'lookup_inventory' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement
Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
Claude executes 'lookup_inventory' directly against the live backend itself

questions.explanation: Claude does not execute tools itself — it emits a tool_use request, and the calling application executes the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result content block.

questions.stem: An application defines a tool named 'calculate_shipping' in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.text: Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
'calculate_shipping' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement
Claude executes 'calculate_shipping' directly against the live backend itself

Claude may respond with a request to call 'calculate_shipping' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message

questions.explanation: Claude does not execute tools itself — it emits a tool_use request, and the calling application executes the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result content block.

questions.stem: Regarding the tool 'get_weather' defined in an API request, select the TWO true statements.

options.text: Claude decides whether and when to call the tool based on the conversation and the tool's description/schema
A single API request can only ever define one tool
The application must execute the tool call and return its result for the conversation to continue meaningfully
Tool results must be sent back as a new 'system' role message

questions.explanation: Claude autonomously decides when a defined tool is relevant (A); multiple tools can be defined per request (so B is false); execution and returning results is the application's job (C); tool results go back as a 'user' message with a tool_result content block, not a system message (so D is false).

questions.stem: A tool executes but raises an exception. How should this be reported back to the model?

options.text: Return a successful result containing an empty value
Return a tool result flagged as an error, describing what went wrong
Abort the conversation and start a new one
Omit the result and send only a user message describing the problem

questions.explanation: Returning a result marked as an error, with a description, lets the model adapt — retry with different arguments, choose another tool, or explain the failure. Silently returning empty success invites wrong conclusions.

questions.stem: A response contains two tool-use blocks. What must the next request include?

options.text: No results, since parallel calls are executed server-side
A result for the first call only, deferring the second
A single merged result covering both calls under one identifier
Results for both calls in the following turn

questions.explanation: Every tool-use block must be answered with its own matching result before the conversation can continue; leaving one unanswered makes the turn incomplete.

questions.stem: What makes a tool description important to the quality of tool use?

options.text: It is shown to end users in the interface
It is used only for API documentation and has no runtime effect
It determines the tool's execution timeout
It is the primary basis on which the model decides whether and how to call the tool

questions.explanation: The description and parameter schema are the model's only information about a tool's purpose and correct use, so vague descriptions are a leading cause of wrong or missing calls.

questions.stem: Select the TWO accurate statements about defining tools on a request.

options.text: The API executes a defined tool automatically and returns its output
Several tools may be defined on a single request and the model chooses among them
Only one tool definition is permitted per request
The model generates the tool's arguments but the application performs the execution

questions.explanation: Multiple tools can be offered and the model selects; it produces the arguments while the caller executes. The API never runs a tool itself, and there is no single-tool limit.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a CLAUDE.md file in a Claude Code project?

options.text: It provides persistent project-level context/instructions (conventions, architecture notes, commands) that Claude Code reads to inform its behavior in that project
It is a required license file with no functional effect
It stores the API key used for authentication
It replaces the need for a settings.json file entirely

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md gives Claude Code durable, project-specific context and instructions so it doesn't need to be re-explained each session.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a custom slash command in Claude Code?

options.text: To permanently modify the underlying model weights
It is purely a cosmetic UI feature with no functional effect
To provide a reusable, named shortcut (e.g., /review) that triggers a predefined prompt or action, so a team can standardize common requests instead of retyping them
To change the pricing tier used for the session

questions.explanation: Slash commands are reusable, named shortcuts for standardizing common, repeatable requests.

questions.stem: A team wants to run a routine code-quality check automatically as part of their CI pipeline, with no live back-and-forth conversation. Which Claude Code interaction mode fits best?

options.text: Interactive mode
Plan mode
Computer use mode
Headless/non-interactive mode, suitable for scripted, one-shot invocations

questions.explanation: Headless/non-interactive mode is designed for scripted, unattended invocations like CI pipeline steps.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of subagents within Claude Code specifically?

options.text: To replace the need for CLAUDE.md entirely
To increase the pricing tier automatically
They serve no functional purpose beyond labeling
To define specialized, narrowly-scoped assistants (e.g., a dedicated test-writer or code-reviewer) that the main session can delegate specific tasks to

questions.explanation: Claude Code subagents let you define specialized, narrowly-scoped assistants for delegated subtasks.

questions.stem: What role do 'hooks' play in Claude Code?

options.text: They allow custom scripts/logic to run automatically at defined points in Claude Code's workflow (e.g., before/after a tool call), enabling custom validation or automation
They are required for every Claude Code project to function at all
They are visual UI themes for the terminal
They control which model tier is billed

questions.explanation: Hooks let developers run custom logic at specific points in Claude Code's execution flow, useful for validation, logging, or automation.

questions.stem: What are 'Skills' in the context of Claude Code / the Claude platform?

options.text: A deprecated feature no longer supported
A billing feature for tracking API cost
A synonym for MCP servers with no meaningful difference
Reusable, packaged instructions/capabilities that can be invoked to guide Claude through a specific type of task consistently

questions.explanation: Skills package reusable instructions/workflows for specific task types, so they can be applied consistently rather than re-explained each time.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of settings.json in Claude Code?

options.text: To store project source code
To configure permissions, tool access, and other behavioral settings for how Claude Code operates in a given project or environment
To define the pricing tier for API usage
It has no functional purpose and is purely documentation

questions.explanation: settings.json is used to configure Claude Code's behavior, including permissions and tool access, at the project or user level.

questions.stem: When an agent's tool call fails in production, what is the recommended debugging approach?

options.text: Ignore the failure since agents are expected to fail occasionally
Assume it is always a transient network issue and retry indefinitely without investigation
Disable all tools going forward
Trace the failure to determine whether it originates in the tool's arguments generated by the model, the tool execution/integration layer, or the external service being called

questions.explanation: Effective debugging isolates whether a failure is in model-generated arguments, the integration/execution layer, or the downstream external service.

questions.stem: A model repeatedly calls a tool with a parameter in the wrong format. Where should investigation begin?

options.text: The output token ceiling, which may be truncating the call
The tool's description and parameter schema, including whether the expected format is stated
The temperature setting, which is probably too high
The model tier, which likely needs upgrading

questions.explanation: The schema and description are the model's only specification of a tool's interface, so systematically malformed arguments usually indicate an underspecified or ambiguous definition.

questions.stem: After deploying a prompt change, an application's output quality appears to regress. What is the best first diagnostic step?

options.text: Immediately assume the underlying model changed and file a support ticket
Add unrelated few-shot examples until the issue disappears
Increase temperature until outputs look better
Run the current and prior prompt versions against a held-out evaluation set to isolate whether the regression traces to the prompt/integration change or something else

questions.explanation: Comparing before/after behavior on a consistent evaluation set is the standard way to isolate whether a regression stems from a specific change.

questions.stem: What is meant by using a 'model-as-judge' approach in evaluation?

options.text: Using only human reviewers with no model involvement
A legal term unrelated to LLM evaluation
Using a separate LLM call to assess/score the quality of another model's output against defined criteria, often to scale evaluation beyond manual review
Letting the model decide its own passing grade with no external criteria

questions.explanation: Model-as-judge uses an LLM to score outputs against defined criteria, allowing evaluation to scale beyond fully manual review.

questions.stem: What is a 'golden dataset' in the context of evaluating an LLM-powered application?

options.text: A dataset containing only failed examples
A dataset that can only be used once and then must be discarded
A curated set of representative inputs with known-good expected outputs, used as a consistent benchmark to measure quality over time or across changes
A dataset of the model's training data

questions.explanation: A golden dataset provides a stable, representative benchmark of inputs with expected outputs for consistent quality measurement across changes.

questions.stem: (Scenario 5) A team wants to catch quality regressions automatically before deploying a new prompt version. What testing practice best supports this?

options.text: Manual, ad hoc spot-checking with no fixed criteria
An automated regression test suite that runs the new prompt against a golden dataset and flags significant deviations before deployment
Skipping testing since prompt changes are low-risk by nature
Only testing after users report problems in production

questions.explanation: Automated regression testing against a stable golden dataset, run pre-deployment, is the standard way to catch quality regressions before they reach users.

questions.stem: A workload is not latency-sensitive and can tolerate being processed within a multi-hour window. Which combination of optimizations would most reduce cost?

options.text: Use synchronous real-time calls to guarantee lowest cost
Use only the largest model with no caching
Use the Message Batches API and apply prompt caching where inputs share static content
Disable caching to simplify the architecture

questions.explanation: Combining Batches API discounts with prompt caching for shared static content stacks cost savings for delay-tolerant, high-repetition workloads.

questions.stem: For 'a customer-facing chatbot' where the top priority is minimizing cost, which model-selection strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Only cost can ever be optimized; latency and quality are fixed regardless of model choice
Ignore the stated priority and choose the same model tier for every use case
Choose model tier and API mode (sync vs. batch) specifically to optimize for cost, while keeping the other factors at an acceptable threshold
Always choose the cheapest option regardless of the stated priority

questions.explanation: Model/API selection should be driven by the specific priority for the use case (cost) while keeping other constraints acceptable — there's no one-size-fits-all model choice.

questions.stem: For 'a high-volume triage classifier' where the top priority is minimizing per-request cost, which factor should weigh most heavily in your model and API configuration choice?

options.text: Selecting a model tier and API mode (synchronous vs. batch, cached vs. uncached) whose cost/latency/quality profile matches 'minimizing per-request cost', rather than defaulting to the same configuration for every workload
The number of tabs open in the developer's browser
Disabling all monitoring to reduce overhead
Always picking the same model regardless of the stated priority, since model choice never affects these factors

questions.explanation: Model and API configuration should be deliberately matched to the workload's actual priority (minimizing per-request cost) rather than using one default setup everywhere.

questions.stem: For 'a high-volume triage classifier' where the top priority is minimizing response latency, which factor should weigh most heavily in your model and API configuration choice?

options.text: The number of tabs open in the developer's browser

Selecting a model tier and API mode (synchronous vs. batch, cached vs. uncached) whose cost/latency/quality profile matches 'minimizing response latency', rather than defaulting to the same configuration for every workload
Always picking the same model regardless of the stated priority, since model choice never affects these factors
Disabling all monitoring to reduce overhead

questions.explanation: Model and API configuration should be deliberately matched to the workload's actual priority (minimizing response latency) rather than using one default setup everywhere.

questions.stem: For 'a high-volume triage classifier' where the top priority is maximizing reasoning quality on ambiguous input, which factor should weigh most heavily in your model and API configuration choice?

options.text: Selecting a model tier and API mode (synchronous vs. batch, cached vs. uncached) whose cost/latency/quality profile matches 'maximizing reasoning quality on ambiguous input', rather than defaulting to the same configuration for every workload
Disabling all monitoring to reduce overhead
Always picking the same model regardless of the stated priority, since model choice never affects these factors
The number of tabs open in the developer's browser

questions.explanation: Model and API configuration should be deliberately matched to the workload's actual priority (maximizing reasoning quality on ambiguous input) rather than using one default setup everywhere.

questions.stem: A nightly job re-scores 200,000 archived documents. Cost matters; completion by morning is sufficient. Which configuration fits best?

options.text: Synchronous calls with streaming enabled
Synchronous calls with extended thinking enabled for accuracy
Synchronous calls at maximum concurrency
Batch submission, accepting asynchronous turnaround for the reduced rate

questions.explanation: High volume with a tolerant deadline is exactly the batch profile: the discount applies and nothing is waiting on the result.

questions.stem: A team proposes routing an interactive support chat through batch processing to halve costs. What is the decisive objection?

options.text: Batch requests are billed at a premium for conversational input
Batch results cannot be parsed programmatically
Batch processing does not support system prompts
Batch turnaround is asynchronous and unsuitable for a user waiting on a reply

questions.explanation: The discount is compensation for relaxed turnaround. A live conversation cannot absorb asynchronous processing, so the saving is unavailable at any acceptable user experience.

questions.stem: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe the batch/synchronous tradeoff.

options.text: Batch reduces per-request cost in exchange for relaxed completion timing
Synchronous requests are the right choice whenever a human is waiting on the output
Batch improves per-request latency compared with synchronous calls
