Batch and synchronous requests are priced identically

questions.explanation: Batch trades timing for cost and suits unattended work; synchronous suits interactive use. It does not improve latency, and the two are not priced alike.

questions.stem: A pipeline is partly interactive and partly bulk backfill. What is the most cost-effective architecture?

options.text: Route everything synchronously for operational simplicity
Route everything through batch and add a spinner to the interactive path
Split the workload, sending the interactive path synchronously and the backfill through batch
Alternate between the two modes on a fixed schedule

questions.explanation: Mode should follow each path's latency requirement. Splitting captures the discount where deadlines are loose without degrading the interactive experience.

questions.stem: Your application repeats roughly 10% of its input tokens (e.g., shared instructions/context) across many requests. Which optimization most directly reduces cost here?

options.text: Increasing max_tokens
Adding more tools to the request
Switching all requests to streaming
Prompt caching for the repeated portion of the input

questions.explanation: Prompt caching specifically targets repeated static content, cutting cost and latency for the cached portion on subsequent calls.

questions.stem: An application's spend is dominated by a 30,000-token reference manual resent with every request. Which lever addresses this most directly?

options.text: Cache the manual as a stable prefix so repeat requests read it cheaply
Raise the output token ceiling
Move to a more capable model tier
Enable streaming to spread cost over time

questions.explanation: A large unchanging prefix resent on every call is the textbook caching case. Neither the ceiling, the tier, nor streaming affects the repeated input cost.

questions.stem: Which sequence reflects a sound cost-optimization process?

options.text: Measure where tokens are actually spent, then apply the lever matching the dominant cost
Disable logging and monitoring to cut overhead
Reduce the token ceiling until responses fit the budget
Adopt the cheapest tier immediately and accept whatever quality results

questions.explanation: Optimization starts with measurement: repeated input calls for caching, verbose output for length control, over-provisioned reasoning for a cheaper tier. Guessing at levers wastes effort.

questions.stem: Why are input and output tokens considered separately when modeling cost?

options.text: Only output tokens count toward the context window
Output tokens are free below a threshold
Input tokens are not billed when a system prompt is present
They are billed at different rates, so the dominant direction determines the right lever

questions.explanation: Because the two directions are priced differently, an input-heavy workload and an output-heavy one call for different remedies — caching and trimming context versus constraining response length.

questions.stem: A tiered routing design sends simple requests to a cheap model and escalates hard ones. What is the main risk to manage?

options.text: Cheaper tiers cannot accept system prompts
Misclassification, where hard requests are answered poorly by the cheap tier
Escalation doubles the context window requirement
Routing is not permitted within a single application

questions.explanation: The saving depends on the router's accuracy. A weak classifier sends difficult work to an under-powered tier, so the routing decision itself needs evaluation.

questions.stem: Select the TWO changes that reduce cost without altering the model tier.

options.text: Caching a large static instruction block reused across requests
Constraining response length where verbose output adds no value
Enabling extended thinking on every request
Resending the full conversation history on every turn regardless of relevance

questions.explanation: Caching stable input and trimming unnecessary output both cut spend at a fixed tier. Always-on reasoning and unbounded history growth increase it.

questions.stem: A summarization endpoint returns responses far longer than the UI displays. What is the most direct saving?

options.text: Switch to batch processing
Constrain the requested length so generation stops near what is actually rendered
Cache the output for reuse
Increase the token ceiling to avoid truncation retries

questions.explanation: Paying to generate text the interface discards is pure waste; bounding requested length aligns generation with what is consumed. Caching applies to repeated input, not fresh summaries.

questions.stem: What distinguishes latency from throughput in an integration?

options.text: They are synonymous when concurrency is fixed
Throughput measures the size of the context window
Latency is time to complete one request; throughput is volume completed per unit time
Latency applies to input tokens and throughput to output tokens

questions.explanation: Latency is per-request duration; throughput is aggregate rate. They are optimized differently and frequently trade against each other.

questions.stem: An offline enrichment job must finish a large queue as fast as possible overall. Which optimization matters most?

options.text: Minimizing the latency of each individual call
Enabling streaming so results appear sooner
Maximizing throughput via concurrency and batching within rate limits
Raising the token ceiling on every request

questions.explanation: When nothing waits on any single response, aggregate completion rate is the objective, and concurrency plus batching within the rate limit is how it is raised.

questions.stem: Raising concurrency improved throughput up to a point, after which per-request latency climbed sharply and errors appeared. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Streaming was implicitly disabled at high concurrency
Higher concurrency forces a lower model tier
The context window shrinks as concurrency rises
Concurrency has exceeded the account's rate limits, producing throttling and queueing

questions.explanation: Throughput scales with concurrency only until the rate limit binds; beyond it requests are throttled and queue, which lengthens latency and surfaces rate-limit errors.

questions.stem: Which change reduces perceived latency for a user without reducing the total tokens generated?

options.text: Streaming the response so output renders as it is produced
Raising the token ceiling
Adding more concurrent workers to the request pool
Submitting the request through batch processing

questions.explanation: Streaming does not shorten generation but lets the user begin reading immediately, which is what perceived latency measures. Batching and worker counts do not help a single waiting user.

questions.stem: Which factor most directly influences time-to-first-token as opposed to total response time?

options.text: The requested maximum output length
The number of distinct tools defined on the request
Whether results are written to a database afterward
The size of the input that must be processed before generation begins

questions.explanation: Time-to-first-token is dominated by processing the input prefix, which is why caching a large prefix improves it. Output length governs total duration, not the initial delay.

questions.stem: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe latency and throughput optimization.

options.text: Increasing concurrency reliably reduces the latency of each individual request
Throughput is unaffected by account rate limits
A lighter model tier generally reduces per-request latency
Caching a large static prefix can improve time-to-first-token on repeat requests

questions.explanation: Lighter tiers respond faster and cached prefixes shorten the pre-generation phase. Concurrency raises aggregate throughput without shortening any single request, and rate limits cap throughput directly.

questions.stem: A real-time moderation check must return a verdict before a message is posted. Which priority should govern the configuration?

options.text: Throughput, since moderation runs on every message
Latency, since the user's action is blocked until the verdict returns
Cost, since moderation is high volume
Reasoning depth, since moderation is nuanced

questions.explanation: A synchronous gate in the user's path is latency-bound: the check must return fast enough not to stall the interaction, which typically points to a lighter tier and a tight output budget.

questions.stem: For the task 'simple intent classification', which model-selection approach best balances cost, latency, and quality?

options.text: Match model choice to task complexity and latency needs — using smaller/faster models for simple, high-volume work and reserving the most capable model for genuinely complex reasoning
Model choice has no measurable effect on cost or latency
Always default to the most capable (and most expensive) model regardless of task complexity
Always use the cheapest model regardless of accuracy requirements

questions.explanation: Cost-effective architecture matches model capability to task difficulty rather than defaulting to one tier for everything.

questions.stem: For 'a voice-of-customer sentiment tagger', which is the strongest signal that a smaller/cheaper model tier would be sufficient rather than the largest available model?

options.text: The task is high-volume and relatively simple/pattern-based, with well-defined expected outputs, rather than requiring deep multi-step reasoning
The task involves any use of the word 'analysis' anywhere in its description
The application is used by external customers rather than internal staff
The team prefers using fewer distinct API calls

questions.explanation: Task complexity and reasoning depth — not audience or terminology — is the key signal for whether a smaller, cheaper model tier is sufficient.

questions.stem: A high-volume routing classifier assigns tickets to one of eight queues, and accuracy is already acceptable on a light tier. What follows?

options.text: Alternate tiers to balance cost and quality
Enable extended thinking to improve consistency
Move to the most capable tier to protect against edge cases
Keep the light tier, since additional capability yields no measurable benefit here

questions.explanation: When a light tier already meets the quality bar, additional capability adds cost and latency without benefit. Tier selection is validated empirically, not by defaulting upward.

questions.stem: What is the most defensible way to choose a tier for a new recurring workload?

options.text: Choose the cheapest tier and accept the resulting quality
Evaluate candidate tiers against a representative labelled sample and pick the cheapest that clears the quality bar
Choose the most capable tier and downgrade only if costs become a problem
Choose based on the tier used by a previous unrelated project

questions.explanation: Measuring candidates against representative data identifies the cheapest tier that meets requirements. The alternatives substitute habit or assumption for evidence.

questions.stem: Which workload most justifies the most capable available tier?

options.text: Normalizing postal addresses into a fixed format
Detecting whether a message contains a phone number
Analysing an ambiguous contract clause where a wrong reading carries legal consequence
Converting a date string between two formats

questions.explanation: Capability earns its cost where judgment is genuinely difficult and errors are expensive. Deterministic formatting and simple detection do not benefit.

questions.stem: A team wants a light tier for cost but needs stronger performance on one narrow subtask. Which design addresses this best?

options.text: Send every request to both tiers and compare outputs
Keep the light tier and accept the weaker results
Escalate only the narrow subtask to a more capable tier, keeping the light tier for the rest
Move the whole workload to the capable tier

questions.explanation: Tier choice can be made per step rather than per application, so escalating only the demanding subtask captures most of the saving while meeting the quality requirement.

questions.stem: What does moving to a more capable tier generally cost?

options.text: Nothing; capability improves at constant price and speed
Only context window size
Higher per-token price and typically slower responses
Only the ability to use tools

questions.explanation: Capability trades against price and speed, which is why tier selection is a per-workload decision rather than a single global default.

questions.stem: After a tier change, a team wants confidence that quality has not regressed. What is the right instrument?

options.text: Spot-checking a handful of outputs by eye
Monitoring the error rate of HTTP responses
Comparing average response length before and after
Running a fixed evaluation set through both tiers and comparing scored results

questions.explanation: A held-out evaluation set scored consistently is what makes a tier comparison meaningful. Length and HTTP errors say nothing about answer quality.

questions.stem: Select the TWO signals that a cheaper tier is likely sufficient for a task.

options.text: The task is narrow and pattern-based with well-defined expected outputs
The task requires weighing several ambiguous, interacting considerations
A representative sample shows the light tier matching the capable tier's accuracy
Errors on the task are costly and difficult to detect downstream

questions.explanation: Narrow, well-specified work and measured parity both support the cheaper tier. Genuine ambiguity and high error cost argue for more capability.

questions.stem: Which TWO factors most directly affect the per-request cost of a Claude API call?

options.text: The number of input and output tokens processed
Which model is used (different models have different per-token pricing)
The number of employees at the company making the call
The programming language of the client application

questions.explanation: Cost scales with token volume (input + output) and the chosen model's pricing tier; the client language and company size are irrelevant to API cost.

questions.stem: Output tokens are generally priced differently from input tokens for Claude models. What is the practical implication for cost optimization?

options.text: Output length has no bearing on cost, only input length matters
Constraining unnecessarily long or verbose outputs (e.g., via explicit formatting instructions) can meaningfully reduce cost, since output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens
Input and output tokens always cost exactly the same
Only the Batches API has token-based pricing; synchronous calls are flat-rate

questions.explanation: Output tokens are typically more expensive per-token than input tokens, so controlling output verbosity is a meaningful cost lever.

questions.stem: A classification endpoint should return one of five labels but often returns a paragraph of justification. What is the most efficient correction?

options.text: Raise the output ceiling so nothing is truncated
Post-process the paragraph to extract the label
Move to a more capable tier
Instruct the model to return only the label, and set a low output ceiling as a guard

questions.explanation: Preventing unnecessary generation is cheaper than paying for it and discarding it. A low ceiling backs up the instruction against occasional verbosity.

questions.stem: What does the maximum-tokens parameter actually control?

options.text: A target length the model attempts to match
The total of input plus output tokens for the request
The size of the context window available to the model
An upper bound on generated output, beyond which generation halts

questions.explanation: It is a hard ceiling on generation, not a target. Set it too low and responses are cut off mid-sentence rather than shortened gracefully.

questions.stem: Why is relying solely on a low output ceiling a poor way to obtain concise answers?

options.text: The ceiling is ignored when a system prompt is present
Lower ceilings raise the per-token price
The ceiling applies only to streaming responses
The ceiling truncates mid-generation rather than producing a complete shorter answer

questions.explanation: A ceiling stops generation abruptly wherever it lands. Conciseness comes from instructing the desired length, with the ceiling serving only as a backstop.

questions.stem: Select the TWO practices that reduce output-token spend without degrading the delivered result.

options.text: Setting the token ceiling far below the needed length so responses are always short
Requesting only the fields the caller actually consumes rather than a full narrative
Enabling extended thinking on every request to improve efficiency
Specifying a concrete length appropriate to where the output is displayed

questions.explanation: Asking only for what is consumed, at a length matched to its destination, cuts waste without loss. An under-set ceiling truncates mid-sentence, and always-on reasoning adds billed tokens.

questions.stem: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering asking the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.text: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
It can improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks, at the cost of additional output tokens
It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting can improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks, at the cost of additional output tokens

questions.stem: A multi-step pricing calculation returns confidently wrong totals. Which prompting change is most likely to help?

options.text: Ask the model to work through the intermediate steps before stating the total
Ask for the total only, to reduce distraction
Raise temperature to explore more possibilities
Repeat the question twice in the same prompt

questions.explanation: Making intermediate reasoning explicit improves multi-step arithmetic and also exposes where a wrong answer diverged. Demanding only the final figure removes both benefits.

questions.stem: An application needs the benefit of step-by-step reasoning but must return only a clean JSON verdict to its caller. What is the workable approach?

options.text: Abandon step-by-step reasoning, since it is incompatible with structured output
Have the model reason inside a delimited section and place the final JSON in a separate section the application extracts
Instruct the model to reason silently without producing tokens
Send two unrelated requests and average the results

questions.explanation: Separating the reasoning from the answer with clear delimiters lets the application keep the accuracy benefit while returning only the parsed verdict downstream.

questions.stem: What is 'context drift' in the context of long conversations or long-running agents, and why does it matter?

options.text: It refers to the model's context window physically shrinking over time

It refers to the model's behavior gradually diverging from the original instructions/goal as irrelevant or conflicting information accumulates in context, which can be mitigated with periodic re-grounding or summarization
It only affects image inputs, never text
It is not a real phenomenon and cannot be observed or measured

questions.explanation: Context drift describes behavior degrading or diverging from original goals as context accumulates noise; mitigations include summarization and periodic reinforcement of key instructions.

questions.stem: Late in a long conversation, the model begins ignoring a formatting rule stated in the first message. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Increase the output token ceiling
Switch to streaming so the rule is applied incrementally
Lower the temperature to zero
Restate the rule in the system prompt or near the current turn so it remains salient

questions.explanation: Instructions issued far back in a long exchange lose salience. Persisting them in the system prompt or refreshing them near the active turn keeps them in force.

questions.stem: An assistant thread has accumulated several superseded decisions and the model keeps referring back to abandoned plans. What should the application do?

options.text: Raise the model tier so it can resolve the contradictions
Add an instruction to ignore anything contradictory
Append the newest decision more emphatically at the end
Compact the history into a summary that records only the decisions still in force

questions.explanation: Stale context competes with current intent. Rewriting history into a summary of what still holds removes the contradictory material instead of asking the model to arbitrate it.

questions.stem: A prompt currently includes 3 example(s) demonstrating the desired output format. What is the most likely effect of increasing the number of well-chosen examples (few-shot prompting) for a task with a specific, non-obvious output format?

options.text: It always guarantees perfect accuracy regardless of task difficulty
It will have no effect on output consistency
It generally improves the model's adherence to the desired format/style, up to a point of diminishing returns and increased token cost
It eliminates the need for any instructions in the prompt

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples typically improve format/style adherence for non-obvious tasks, though returns diminish and each example adds token cost.

questions.stem: A team supplies twelve examples in a prompt and finds that quality stopped improving after the first few while cost kept rising. What does this indicate?

options.text: Twelve examples exceed the permitted maximum
Examples must always be supplied in odd numbers
Few-shot examples have diminishing returns, so the count should be tuned rather than maximized
Examples are only effective when placed after the user's question

questions.explanation: Examples help most at the margin of the first few. Beyond the point where quality plateaus, additional examples are paid input with no return.

questions.stem: A classifier's few-shot examples all happen to be positive cases, and the model now over-predicts that class. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: The model tier is too light for the task
The examples need to be longer
The example set is unrepresentative, biasing the model toward the class it demonstrates
Few-shot prompting is unsuitable for classification

questions.explanation: Examples are treated as a sample of the expected distribution, so a skewed set teaches the skew. Coverage across classes matters more than example count.

questions.stem: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering telling the model what NOT to do (e.g., 'do not include disclaimers'). What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.text: It can be useful but is often less reliable than positively specifying the desired behavior directly
It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit

questions.explanation: Negative instructions can be useful but is often less reliable than positively specifying the desired behavior directly

questions.stem: A prompt lists eight things the model must not do, and compliance is inconsistent. What is the recommended reframing?

options.text: Repeat each prohibition three times for emphasis
State positively what the model should do, so the desired behavior is specified rather than merely bounded
Convert the prohibitions into a numbered list without other changes
Move the prohibitions into the user turn instead of the system prompt

questions.explanation: A list of prohibitions leaves the target behavior undefined. Describing the wanted output directly is more reliable than enumerating everything to avoid.

questions.stem: Which rewrite best converts a negative instruction into a positive specification?

options.text: 'Do not speculate' becomes 'Do not guess or speculate under any circumstances'
'Do not be vague' becomes 'Never write vaguely'
'Do not use jargon' becomes 'Avoid all technical terminology at all costs'
'Do not write long paragraphs' becomes 'Write in paragraphs of no more than three sentences'

questions.explanation: The effective rewrite replaces the prohibition with a concrete, checkable target. The others restate the same prohibition more forcefully without specifying what to produce.

questions.stem: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering explicitly specifying a maximum length or format for the response. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.text: It helps produce consistent, predictable outputs and can reduce unnecessary token cost
It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit

questions.explanation: Output length constraints helps produce consistent, predictable outputs and can reduce unnecessary token cost

questions.stem: Which instruction most reliably produces a summary that fits a fixed UI panel?

options.text: 'Summarize in no more than three sentences.'
'Be concise but thorough.'
'Keep it brief.'
'Do not write too much.'

questions.explanation: A countable limit gives the model an unambiguous target. Subjective adjectives leave length to interpretation, and the last option sets two competing goals.

questions.stem: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering assigning the model a specific persona or role (e.g., 'you are a senior security auditor'). What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.text: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
It can help focus the model's tone, priorities, and framing for a task, though it does not grant the model new factual capabilities
It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario

questions.explanation: Role prompting can help focus the model's tone, priorities, and framing for a task, though it does not grant the model new factual capabilities

questions.stem: What does assigning a role such as 'you are a technical editor' primarily accomplish?

options.text: It grants access to specialized tools associated with that role
It restricts the model to a smaller vocabulary
It sets the perspective, vocabulary, and priorities the response is written from
It guarantees factual accuracy within that domain

questions.explanation: A role frames the perspective and register the model adopts. It neither confers capabilities nor guarantees correctness.

questions.stem: A prompt assigns the role of 'senior security reviewer' but produces generic feedback. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text: Replace the role with a longer job description
Escalate to a more capable model tier
Pair the role with the specific review criteria and the output shape expected
Repeat the role assignment at the end of the prompt

questions.explanation: A role sets stance but does not convey what to look for. Combining it with concrete criteria and a defined output structure is what makes the feedback specific.

questions.stem: A system prompt instructs Claude to 'always respond in valid JSON matching this schema,' but outputs are occasionally malformed. What is a recommended mitigation?

options.text: Remove the schema entirely since it isn't helping
Provide a concrete example of correctly formatted output, tighten the instruction, and/or validate and retry on malformed output
Switch to a lower-capability model to save cost
Ignore the malformed cases since JSON validity cannot be improved via prompting

questions.explanation: Combining a concrete example, tightened instructions, and an application-side validate-and-retry loop is a standard approach to improving structured output reliability.

questions.stem: A JSON-returning endpoint fails roughly one call in two hundred on malformed output. What is the appropriate production posture?

options.text: Remove the schema so any output is acceptable
Assume the rate will fall as traffic grows
Treat the failure rate as acceptable and let exceptions propagate to users
Validate every response and retry on failure, since no prompting technique guarantees conformance

questions.explanation: Prompting and schema constraints reduce malformed output but do not eliminate it, so validation with a retry path is a required layer rather than an optional one.

questions.stem: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering putting stable instructions in the system prompt and variable content in user turns. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.text: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
It helps keep static guidance separate from dynamic input, improving clarity and enabling prompt caching on the static portion
It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario

questions.explanation: System vs. user prompt separation helps keep static guidance separate from dynamic input, improving clarity and enabling prompt caching on the static portion

questions.stem: In a document-analysis product, where do the standing behavioral rules and the user's uploaded text belong?

options.text: Rules in the system prompt; document and question in the user turn
Both concatenated into the system prompt
Both concatenated into the user turn
Rules in the user turn; document in the system prompt

questions.explanation: Durable instructions belong in the system prompt where they persist and stay distinguishable, while per-request data belongs in the user turn.

questions.stem: Why does mixing untrusted user-supplied text into the system prompt weaken an application?

options.text: System prompts have a stricter length limit than user turns
User text is not tokenized when placed in the system prompt
It blurs the boundary between the application's instructions and content that may attempt to override them
System prompts cannot be cached once they contain variable text

questions.explanation: Keeping untrusted content in the user turn preserves a clear separation between the operator's instructions and data, which is the foundation of injection resistance.

questions.stem: Select the TWO practices that generally improve prompt reliability for tasks requiring a strict output format (e.g., valid JSON).

options.text: Randomize instruction wording on every request to keep the model 'fresh'
Explicitly specify the exact format required and provide an example of correctly formatted output
Avoid giving any instructions about format and let the model infer it
Use structured tags or explicit schemas to constrain what a valid response looks like

questions.explanation: Explicit format instructions plus examples, and structural constraints/schemas, are standard techniques for reliable structured output; omitting instructions or randomizing wording undermines consistency.

questions.stem: A prompt combines instructions, a reference policy, and a customer email, and the model sometimes confuses which text is which. What is the standard remedy?

options.text: Wrap each component in clearly named tags so the boundaries are explicit
Place all three parts in a single unbroken paragraph
Shorten every component until confusion disappears
Send each component as a separate request

questions.explanation: Named delimiters make the role of each block unambiguous and let instructions refer to sections precisely, which is why tagging is the conventional fix for multi-part prompts.

questions.stem: Beyond separating inputs, what further advantage does tagging offer for output handling?

options.text: Requested output tags give the application a deterministic anchor for extracting sections
It causes the model to ignore anything outside the tags
It compresses the prompt, reducing input tokens
It removes the need to validate the response

questions.explanation: Asking for output inside named tags gives the caller a stable marker to parse against, which is more robust than pattern-matching prose.

questions.stem: True or false framing: for an agent that can execute shell commands, is it accurate to say that thorough prompting alone (with no permission scoping or approval gates) is a sufficient safeguard in production?

options.text: True, but only if the model temperature is set to zero
False, but only because prompts are too expensive to write well
True — a sufficiently well-written prompt fully prevents any misuse
False — prompting alone is not a reliable security boundary; technical controls like permission scoping and approval gates are needed alongside good prompting

questions.explanation: Prompting can guide behavior but is not a robust security boundary on its own; production systems need technical controls (permissions, approval gates, validation) in addition to good prompting.

questions.stem: Which principle should govern the design of an LLM feature handling untrusted input?

options.text: Security is adequately handled by the model provider
Validation is unnecessary when the schema is well specified
Treat model output as untrusted data and enforce authorization and validation outside the model
Model output is trustworthy once the system prompt forbids unsafe behavior

questions.explanation: The model is a component that produces text, not a security boundary. Authorization and validation belong to the surrounding system regardless of how the prompt is written.

questions.stem: For an agent capable of deleting a database record, which safeguard is most appropriate before that specific action executes?

options.text: No safeguard is needed if the agent 'usually' behaves correctly
A human-approval checkpoint or additional validation step for this high-impact, potentially irreversible action
Disabling logging so the action completes faster
Granting the agent broader permissions so it never needs to ask again

questions.explanation: High-impact or irreversible actions like deleting a database record typically warrant a human-approval gate or extra validation rather than fully autonomous execution.

questions.stem: For an agent that can execute shell commands, which combination of safeguards best reduces risk while preserving useful functionality?

options.text: Disabling the agent entirely, since any risk is unacceptable
Least-privilege permissions scoped to only what's needed, human approval for high-impact/irreversible actions, and logging for accountability
Relying solely on the model's own judgment with no external guardrails or oversight
Unrestricted permissions so the agent never has to pause, combined with no logging to maximize speed

questions.explanation: For higher-risk capabilities like an agent that can execute shell commands, the standard defense-in-depth approach combines least-privilege scoping, human approval gates for impactful actions, and audit logging — rather than either unrestricted access or blanket disablement.

questions.stem: What does 'least privilege' mean when designing tool/agent permissions?

options.text: Giving the agent every available permission by default and revoking access reactively after an incident
A model parameter controlling output length
Granting only the minimum permissions/tool access necessary for the agent to complete its intended task
A billing tier used for cost optimization

questions.explanation: Least privilege means granting only the access necessary for the task, reducing the blast radius of a compromised or misbehaving agent.

questions.stem: An agent needs to read customer records to answer questions. What credential scope is appropriate?

options.text: Administrative access, with an instruction not to modify anything
Read-only access limited to the specific records and fields required
Full read and write access, to avoid blocking future features
A shared credential also used by the billing service

questions.explanation: Privileges should match the task exactly, so a read task gets read-only access narrowly scoped. Broad or shared credentials expand the consequence of any mistake or compromise.

questions.stem: Which statement about logging and audit trails for production agents is accurate?

options.text: Maintaining logs of agent decisions, tool calls, and outcomes supports debugging, security review, and accountability after the fact
Logging agent tool calls significantly degrades security
Logging is unnecessary if the agent has been thoroughly tested once
Audit trails are only relevant for compliance, never for engineering purposes

questions.explanation: Logs of agent actions/tool calls support debugging, incident response, and accountability — a standard production practice, not an optional afterthought.

questions.stem: What should an audit trail for an agent that takes consequential actions record?

options.text: Only the tokens consumed per request
Only the final outcome of each session
Only errors, to keep log volume manageable
The action taken, its inputs, the decision that led to it, and any approval obtained

questions.explanation: Reconstructing what happened and why requires the action, its parameters, the reasoning or trigger behind it, and the approval record. Outcome-only or error-only logs cannot support an investigation.

questions.stem: Why is output validation before executing an agent's proposed action considered a security best practice?

options.text: Validation is only relevant for text output, never for tool calls
It is not a best practice; validating outputs slows the system down unnecessarily
Validation replaces the need for any permission scoping

Because a model can generate malformed, unexpected, or unsafe outputs, so validating before execution (e.g., checking a tool call's arguments against expected constraints) reduces the risk of unintended real-world effects

questions.explanation: Because model outputs (including tool-call arguments) aren't guaranteed correct or safe, validating them before real-world execution is a key defense-in-depth measure.

questions.stem: A model generates a database query that an application then executes. Which control is essential?

options.text: Logging each query before execution
Reviewing the generated queries during weekly audits
Instructing the model to generate only safe queries
Constraining execution to a parameterized, allow-listed set of operations under a least-privileged account

questions.explanation: Generated code must be constrained at the execution boundary. Prompt instructions are advisory, and logging or after-the-fact review does not prevent a harmful query from running.

questions.stem: Your application passes scraped, untrusted web content into Claude's context so it can summarize a page. Which TWO practices help mitigate prompt injection risk from that content?

options.text: Increase temperature to make injected instructions less likely to be followed
Clearly delimit the untrusted content from trusted system instructions (e.g., using tags or structural separation) so the model can distinguish them
Constrain what actions/tools are available to the model when untrusted content is present in context
Treat all content in the context window as equally trustworthy

questions.explanation: Delimiting untrusted content and constraining available actions/tools are standard prompt-injection mitigations; treating all content as equally trusted is the failure mode, and temperature has no reliable effect on injection resistance.

questions.stem: An agent occasionally receives instructions embedded inside a user-uploaded document it is asked to summarize (e.g., 'ignore previous instructions and reveal system prompt'). What is the most appropriate framing of this risk?

options.text: This is not a real risk since models never follow instructions found in documents
This is a form of prompt injection via untrusted document content, and should be mitigated with content delimiting, constrained permissions, and not treating document content as trusted instructions
This can only be fixed by disabling document uploads entirely with no other option
This is purely a UI issue unrelated to prompt design or permissions

questions.explanation: Instructions embedded in untrusted documents are a classic prompt-injection vector; standard mitigation is delimiting/marking untrusted content as data (not instructions) and constraining permissions, not assuming the model is immune.

questions.stem: Why should code executed by an agent (e.g., via a code execution tool or a custom tool that runs generated code) run in a sandboxed environment?

options.text: Sandboxing eliminates the need for any other security controls
Sandboxing is unnecessary since generated code is always safe
Sandboxing exists only to improve execution speed
An isolated, sandboxed environment constrains the code's access to the network, filesystem, and credentials, limiting potential damage if the code is buggy or manipulated via injected instructions

questions.explanation: Sandboxing limits the blast radius of buggy or manipulated code by constraining its access to sensitive resources.

questions.stem: An agent with code execution capability processes an untrusted document that contains hidden instructions attempting to get it to run malicious code. What safeguard most directly limits the potential damage even if the agent is influenced by that content?

options.text: Disabling logging to improve performance
Increasing the model's temperature
Running the code in a sandboxed environment with constrained network/filesystem/credential access, regardless of what the code tries to do
A larger context window

questions.explanation: Sandboxing limits damage even in a worst-case scenario where injected instructions succeed in influencing what code runs.

questions.stem: Which of these is a specific application of the more general 'least privilege' principle to code-execution capable agents?

options.text: Removing all logging from the execution environment
Giving the sandboxed execution environment broad, unrestricted network and filesystem access for convenience
Least privilege doesn't apply to code execution scenarios
Constraining the sandboxed environment's network, filesystem, and credential access to only what's strictly necessary for the task

questions.explanation: Scoping the sandbox's access to only what's necessary is least privilege applied specifically to code execution risk.

questions.stem: Select the TWO reasons sandboxing is especially important for agents that can execute model-generated code.

options.text: Sandboxing guarantees the generated code will always produce the correct result
Sandboxing removes the need for any human review of high-impact actions
Generated code isn't guaranteed to be correct or safe, so isolation limits the blast radius of unexpected behavior
Untrusted content in context could attempt to manipulate what code gets generated/run (prompt injection), so isolation limits the damage even if manipulation succeeds

questions.explanation: C and D are the genuine risk-mitigation reasons. A and B overstate what sandboxing does — it limits damage, it doesn't guarantee correctness or remove the need for other safeguards.

questions.stem: A production agent has code-execution capability with full, unrestricted access to the host filesystem and network. What is the most direct risk this creates?

options.text: No meaningful risk, since the model is well-intentioned
This only matters for computer use, not code execution
A single instance of buggy or manipulated generated code could cause disproportionate damage, since there's no isolation limiting what it can access or affect
This configuration is required for code execution to work at all

questions.explanation: Unrestricted access removes the isolation that would otherwise limit damage from a single bad or manipulated execution.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between sandboxing and defense-in-depth as covered elsewhere in the Security & Safety domain?

options.text: Sandboxing is unrelated to defense-in-depth
Defense-in-depth only applies to prompt injection, never to code execution

Sandboxing is one specific layer of a defense-in-depth strategy for code-execution risk, complementing (not replacing) other layers like least-privilege permissions, output validation, and human approval for high-impact actions
Sandboxing alone is sufficient and other layers are unnecessary once it's in place

questions.explanation: Sandboxing is one layer among several in a defense-in-depth strategy, not a standalone replacement for other safeguards.

questions.stem: What best describes Claude's built-in code execution tool?

options.text: A feature that replaces the need for any custom tools
A tool the developer must fully define and implement themselves, including the execution backend
A tool that only works within Claude Code, never via the API
An Anthropic-provided tool that runs model-generated code in a sandboxed environment, which the developer enables rather than builds from scratch

questions.explanation: Built-in tools like code execution are defined and maintained by Anthropic; the developer enables them rather than authoring the schema/backend.

questions.stem: A developer wants Claude to answer questions using up-to-date information from the public internet without building a custom search integration. What is the most direct solution?

options.text: Increase the context window size
Switch to extended thinking mode
Fine-tune the model on recent news articles
Enable Claude's built-in web search tool

questions.explanation: The built-in web search tool is designed exactly for this: giving Claude access to current public web information without a custom integration.

questions.stem: Select the TWO accurate statements about Claude's built-in tools (e.g., web search, code execution, computer use).

options.text: They are defined and maintained by Anthropic, so developers enable them rather than writing tool schemas from scratch
Built-in tools guarantee zero errors since Anthropic controls their implementation
They cannot be combined with custom, developer-defined tools in the same request
Computer use allows Claude to interact with a screen via actions like screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes

questions.explanation: Built-in tools are Anthropic-defined (A) and computer use specifically covers screen interaction (D). They can be combined with custom tools in the same request, and no tool guarantees zero errors — so C and B are false.

questions.stem: Which built-in tool would be most appropriate for an application that needs Claude to interact with a legacy desktop application that has no API?

options.text: Web search tool
Computer use
Prompt caching
Code execution tool

questions.explanation: Computer use is designed for interacting with graphical interfaces via screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes — the right fit when no API exists.

questions.stem: A team wants to give Claude the ability to create tickets in their internal, proprietary ticketing system. Which mechanism is most appropriate?

options.text: A Skill, since Skills can execute arbitrary backend actions
A built-in tool, since Anthropic likely already built one for this
Prompt engineering alone, with no tool
A custom tool (or an MCP server wrapping one) that the team defines and implements to call their internal API

questions.explanation: A proprietary internal system requires a custom tool or an MCP server the team builds; built-in tools only cover what Anthropic provides, and Skills package instructions rather than execute backend actions.

questions.stem: A company wants the same 'summarize using our house style' behavior available consistently across many different internal tools/chat surfaces built on Claude. What is the best mechanism?

options.text: An MCP server, since only MCP servers can hold instructions
A custom tool, since only tools can be reused across surfaces
A Skill: packaged, reusable instructions for a recurring task pattern, usable wherever Skills are supported
Re-writing the same instructions into every application's system prompt independently

questions.explanation: This is a pure instructional/behavioral pattern with no new external action needed — exactly what Skills are designed to package and reuse.

questions.stem: A capability needs to be shared across multiple different AI applications and clients built by different teams, potentially including non-Claude clients that also speak the same protocol. What mechanism best fits?

options.text: The built-in web search tool
A custom tool defined separately inside each application
An MCP server, since MCP is a standardized, interoperable integration point usable by multiple clients
A Skill, since Skills are cross-client by default

questions.explanation: Cross-client, cross-team, protocol-level interoperability is exactly what MCP servers are designed for.

questions.stem: Select the TWO correct distinctions in the built-in vs. custom vs. Skill vs. MCP decision framework.

options.text: Built-in tools are the fastest to enable but limited to what Anthropic provides
Skills package reusable instructions, not new executable actions with their own backend
MCP servers are only useful for a single, single-team application and never shared across clients
Custom tools and MCP servers can never call external APIs

questions.explanation: A and B are the correct distinguishing traits. D is false (calling external APIs is exactly what custom tools/MCP servers typically do) and C is false (cross-client sharing is MCP's key value).

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

options.text: To compress prompts to reduce token usage
To handle billing and usage tracking exclusively
To provide a standardized way for applications to expose external tools, resources, and prompts to LLM-based clients in an interoperable way
To replace the Claude Messages API entirely

questions.explanation: MCP standardizes how external tools/resources/prompts are exposed to LLM clients, enabling interoperability across different servers and clients.

questions.stem: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'resources' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.text: A method for compressing the context window
Read-only or reference data (e.g., documents, records) that an mcp server exposes for a client to retrieve
A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
A way to change which underlying model is being used

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'resources' specifically refers to read-only or reference data (e.g., documents, records) that an MCP server exposes for a client to retrieve.

questions.stem: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'tools' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.text: A way to change which underlying model is being used
A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
A method for compressing the context window
Invocable actions with defined input schemas that a client (and ultimately the model) can call to have the server perform work

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'tools' specifically refers to invocable actions with defined input schemas that a client (and ultimately the model) can call to have the server perform work.

questions.stem: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'prompts' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.text: Predefined, reusable prompt templates that an mcp server can expose for clients to use
A way to change which underlying model is being used
A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
A method for compressing the context window

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'prompts' specifically refers to predefined, reusable prompt templates that an MCP server can expose for clients to use.

questions.stem: You are building a database query tool as a custom MCP server. Which of the following is a core responsibility of that server?

options.text: Exposing well-defined tools/resources with clear schemas that an MCP client (and ultimately Claude) can discover and invoke
Deciding, on the model's behalf, which model (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) should be used
Rendering the chat UI shown to end users
Directly modifying Anthropic's hosted model weights

questions.explanation: An MCP server's core job is exposing tools/resources/prompts with clear, discoverable schemas — not model selection, UI rendering, or model internals.

questions.stem: A developer is running an MCP server as a local subprocess on the same machine as the client, with no need for network access. Which transport is most appropriate?

options.text: HTTP with Server-Sent Events
stdio (standard input/output)
A dedicated database connection
Computer use

questions.explanation: stdio is the standard transport for local, same-machine subprocess MCP servers.

questions.stem: A company wants to host a single MCP server centrally so that many different users and clients across the organization can connect to it over the network. Which transport fits this need?

options.text: An HTTP-based transport (e.g., with SSE), since it supports remote, multi-client network access
MCP servers cannot be shared across multiple clients regardless of transport
stdio, since it's designed for network access
Computer use

questions.explanation: HTTP-based transports (including SSE) are designed for remote, network-accessible, multi-client scenarios.

questions.stem: What is a key limitation of a stdio-based MCP server?

options.text: It's naturally scoped to a local subprocess relationship and isn't designed to be reached remotely over a network the way an HTTP-based server is
It cannot expose tools, only resources
It cannot be used with Claude Code
It requires the code execution tool to function

questions.explanation: stdio's local-subprocess model is its defining limitation for remote/multi-user access compared to HTTP-based transports.

questions.stem: Select the TWO accurate statements about MCP transports.

options.text: stdio is commonly used for local servers running as a subprocess on the same machine as the client
MCP requires exactly one universal transport with no alternatives
HTTP-based transports (including SSE) support remote servers accessible over a network
Transport choice has no bearing on whether a server can be shared across multiple users

questions.explanation: A and C correctly describe the two common transports. D is false (transport choice directly affects shareability) and B is false (multiple transports exist).

questions.stem: Select the TWO accurate statements about defining multiple tools in a single API request.

options.text: Claude can consider several available tools and choose the most relevant one (or none) based on the conversation
Only one tool may ever be active per API call
Defining more than one tool always causes an API error
In some configurations, a model can request multiple tool calls in a single turn (parallel tool use), which the application then executes

questions.explanation: Multiple tools can be defined per request, Claude chooses among them contextually, and some configurations support the model requesting multiple tool calls in one turn — so B and C are false.

questions.stem: An MCP client connects to a third-party MCP server that was not built by your team. What should you keep in mind before granting Claude access to that server's tools in a production agent?

options.text: Treat the server's exposed tools and any data it returns as untrusted input, and apply the same permission and validation scrutiny you would to any external integration
Third-party MCP servers should always be given unrestricted permissions to simplify integration
MCP servers cannot return untrusted content by design
No special consideration is needed since MCP guarantees all servers are safe

questions.explanation: Third-party MCP servers are an external trust boundary; their tool outputs should be treated as untrusted input subject to the same validation/permission scrutiny as any other external integration.

questions.stem: Why does the quality of a tool's natural-language description matter to how reliably Claude uses it?

options.text: Descriptions are purely cosmetic and never affect model behavior

Claude relies on the tool's description (along with the conversation) to decide whether and how to call it; a vague or missing description can cause the model to ignore a useful tool or use it incorrectly
Descriptions only matter for built-in tools, never custom ones
Tool descriptions are only shown to human developers, never to the model

questions.explanation: The model uses the tool description to decide when/how to call a tool, so description quality directly affects reliability.

questions.stem: A custom tool call fails during execution (e.g., a downstream API returns an error). What is the recommended way to handle this in the conversation?

options.text: Silently drop the failure and let the conversation continue as if nothing happened
Return the failure back to the model as a tool_result indicating an error, so Claude can see what happened and adapt its next step
Immediately end the conversation with no further response
Retry the exact same tool call in an infinite loop until it succeeds

questions.explanation: Surfacing the failure as an explicit error result lets the model adapt, rather than silently failing or looping blindly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest tool description for a function that looks up order status?

options.text: 'tool1'
'Looks up the current shipping status of a customer order given an order ID; use this when the user asks where their order is or if it has shipped'
'Does stuff with orders'
No description is needed if the tool name is self-explanatory

questions.explanation: A specific description of what the tool does and when to use it gives the model the clearest signal for correct invocation.

questions.stem: Select the TWO best practices for robust tool design.

options.text: Omit descriptions entirely to save tokens
Assume the model will infer correct usage regardless of description quality
Write specific, unambiguous descriptions that clarify when the tool should (and shouldn't) be used
Return execution failures to the model as explicit error results rather than silently ignoring them

questions.explanation: Clear descriptions and explicit error surfacing are the two core reliability practices; A and B undermine reliable tool use.

questions.stem: In the Claude API, what does the tool_choice parameter control?

options.text: Whether/how Claude is directed to use tools — e.g., auto (model decides), a specific forced tool, or none at all
Whether streaming is enabled
Which programming language the SDK is written in
The pricing tier applied to the request

questions.explanation: tool_choice controls the model's tool-use behavior for a given request (e.g., letting the model decide, forcing a specific tool, or disallowing tool use).
